summary: The paper simulates K institutions independently screening a shared applicant pool under a shared/idiosyncratic noise decomposition (weight sqrt(rho) vs sqrt(1-rho)), showing a homogenization metric H grows with rho while per-institution accuracy stays flat (confirming Kleinberg & Raghavan's theoretical point in simulation), and then sweeps a randomized-lottery decorrelation mitigation to trace an accuracy-homogenization tradeoff, headlined by the corrected claim that fully undoing rho=0.8 monoculture costs ~22% relative accuracy (eta~0.35, accuracy 0.568->~0.44). This is a revision responding to a prior review that flagged two numerical errors (a mistranscribed Student-t column in Table 1, and an incorrect eta~0.47/~30%-cost headline figure); I re-ran sim.py end-to-end and independently reproduced results.json, then checked every number quoted in the text (Table 1 Gaussian and Student-t columns, K-ablation, p-ablation, the anchor_K4 systemic-rejection figures, and both the Gaussian and Student-t mitigation-sweep interpolations) directly against results.json, and all of them now match, including the corrected eta~0.35/accuracy~0.44/~22% figure which I re-derived independently via linear interpolation and got the same numbers.
strengths:
- Fully reproducible: `python sim.py` regenerates results.json in ~18s on CPU, and I independently verified every headline statistic quoted in the abstract, Table 1, the K/p ablations, and the mitigation-sweep interpolation (eta~0.35, accuracy~0.44, ~22% relative cost) against a fresh run of the code -- no discrepancies found this round
- The revision transparently corrects two errors a prior review identified (the mistranscribed Table 1 Student-t column and the eta~0.47/~30%-cost headline figure that didn't follow from results.json), and explicitly documents the correction and re-verification process in the text rather than silently fixing it
- Clean, minimal, well-specified model (shared vs. idiosyncratic noise, deterministic SHA-256-derived seeding, 30 seeds/cell, Bonferroni-adjusted significance) that cleanly isolates homogenization from per-institution accuracy, with reasonable robustness sweeps (Gaussian vs. Student-t noise, K in {4,8,16}, p in {0.1,0.2,0.4}) that all check out against the code
weaknesses:
- Novelty is modest and the paper says so itself: it is a parameterized re-simulation of Bommasani et al. (2022)'s shared/idiosyncratic noise model plus a mitigation sweep, with no new theoretical result and no real-data experiment; the anchor to Bommasani et al. (2026) is explicitly only qualitative/directional (rho=0 vs rho>0 regimes), not a fitted numeric correspondence, so the paper's practical takeaway is bounded by a toy model whose rho is not empirically calibrated
- The lottery mitigation (fully random Bernoulli(p) replacement of institutional decisions with probability eta) is acknowledged as a blind, unrealistic baseline policy, and the paper does not simulate or compare it against any more targeted decorrelation strategy, so the accuracy-cost figure characterizes one somewhat contrived intervention rather than anything closer to a deployable policy
- Table 1 displays a single shared Accuracy column even though results.json shows Student-t accuracy (~0.630-0.647) is substantially higher than Gaussian accuracy (~0.568-0.571) at the same rho -- the text's claim that 'Recall@p stays within [0.568, 0.571] across the entire rho sweep' is true only for the Gaussian condition, and the table's layout (one Accuracy column next to two H columns) could mislead a reader into assuming accuracy is distribution-invariant as well as rho-invariant, which the underlying data does not support
questions:
1. Why does Student-t accuracy (~0.63-0.65) run noticeably higher than Gaussian accuracy (~0.57) at matched rho -- is this an artifact of the unit-variance rescaling of the Student-t noise, and if so is recall@p comparable across the two noise conditions at all?
2. Have you tried simulating even a simple targeted decorrelation (e.g., only intervening on the subset of institutions sharing a vendor cluster) to see whether it beats the blind lottery's accuracy-homogenization tradeoff, as the conclusion suggests is the natural next step?
3. Given that the rho used in the simulation is not fit to Bommasani et al. (2026)'s real hiring data (only qualitatively anchored), how sensitive is the headline ~22% accuracy-cost figure to the choice of rho=0.8 as the 'high monoculture' operating point, versus, say, rho=0.5 or rho=0.6?
